Summary  
Data source overview: The paper critically examines widely-used saliency (feature-attribution) methods. It shows, with theory and experiments, that several popular techniques produce nearly identical explanations even after the model parameters or training data are randomised, revealing that these methods are effectively independent of the model and the data. The authors propose a set of “sanity-check” sensitivity tests—based on parameter and data randomisation—as a principled way to vet saliency methods before using them for debugging, outlier detection or scientific explanation. They supply empirical and theoretical evidence supporting the approach.  

Inference strategy justification: The text makes explicit claims about the failure modes of certain saliency methods, the need for sensitivity tests, and the experimental/theoretical support for the proposed methodology. Where the text is concise, moderate inference was used only to formulate practical interventions (e.g., integrating the tests into a pre-deployment workflow), marked with confidence level 2 and explained in the rationales.  

Extraction completeness explanation: All causal chains from the top-level risk (misleading explanations) through problem analysis, theoretical insight, design rationale, implementation mechanism and validation evidence to two actionable interventions are captured. Nodes are named at the canonical granularity recommended so they can merge readily with other sources on interpretability testing. Every node is connected; no isolated or duplicate nodes remain.  

Key limitations: 1) The paper excerpt lacks formal section headings, so rationales cite inferred sections (“Abstract”, “Experiments”, “Theory”). 2) Interventions are practical extrapolations rather than instructions explicitly listed by the authors; they are therefore assigned lower evidence confidence. 3) The fabric focuses on interpretability and does not touch downstream socio-technical risks which may be discussed elsewhere.  

EXTRACTION CONFIDENCE[83] – high confidence in node/edge correctness and JSON validity; moderate uncertainty arises from missing section headers and implicit interventions. The instruction set could be improved by clarifying how to reference rationales when explicit section titles are absent and by giving more guidance on selecting edge verbs when several apply equally.
